strengths: Identifies and formalizes a genuinely novel and previously unstudied failure mode of t-SNE (false positive clusters, outlier suppression), complementing the existing positive guarantees of Arora et al. (2018) and Linderman & Steinerberger (2019); the paper convincingly argues this is the first theoretical treatment of these limitations.

The core technical insight — t-SNE's invariance under additive shifts of squared interpoint distances (Lemma 16, via Schoenberg's embedding theorem) — is clean and yields surprisingly strong consequences: impostor datasets with arbitrarily low silhouette scores producing identical stationary point sets (Theorem 3), neighborhoods of the regular simplex generating ALL possible stationary outputs (Lemma 6), and an input-agnostic upper bound on depictable outlier extremity (Theorem 8).

Theoretical results are well complemented by practical demonstrations on real datasets (PBMC3k single-cell data, credit card fraud, BBC News embeddings), including a concrete impostor-construction algorithm (Algorithm 1) and a single-poison-point adversarial attack that destroys cluster structure.

Discussion is balanced: the authors acknowledge that additive invariance may confer robustness to random noise due to concentration of measure, and provide supporting experiments (Figure 6), rather than presenting a purely negative story.
Paper is clearly written with good intuition (e.g., the nearest-neighbor-graph vs. radius-neighborhood-graph explanation of input/output affinity asymmetry) and complete proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The central observation (additive invariance) is elementary, and the main theorems follow from relatively simple continuity/intermediate-value arguments; the technical depth is limited, which may reduce the contribution's weight relative to its framing.

All theoretical guarantees concern the set of stationary points of the plain KL objective (Definition 1), whereas practical t-SNE uses early exaggeration and gradient descent dynamics; the paper does not formally connect its stationary-point analysis to the embeddings actually returned in practice (the empirical results partially mitigate this but the theory-practice gap is not analyzed).

The negative results are somewhat expected from practitioner folklore ('t-SNE exaggerates clusters' is widely anecdotally known, e.g., Chari & Pachter 2023, Wattenberg et al.); the value lies mainly in the formalization, and the significance of the formalization over existing empirical critiques could be argued further.

The quantitative empirical evaluation is relatively thin: most evidence is qualitative scatter plots with silhouette scores; no systematic comparison against other embedding methods (UMAP, TriMap) is provided even though these are discussed in related work, and outlier results are compared only against PCA.

Reproducibility is undermined by the incomplete GitHub link in Section 4 (the URL appears blank in the manuscript), and several experimental details (t-SNE hyperparameters such as perplexity, learning rate, number of iterations used in the real-data experiments) are not reported in the main text.

The outlier definition (Definition 7) and Theorem 8 consider only a single outlier; the multi-outlier phenomena emphasized empirically (Figures 4 and 5) are not covered by theory, and the constant '8' in Theorem 8's bound appears somewhat arbitrary without discussion of tightness.

strengths: The central question — whether a clustered t-SNE output implies a clustered input — is well-motivated and complementary to existing positive results (Arora et al., 2018; Linderman & Steinerberger, 2019); the paper fills a genuine gap by providing the first systematic theoretical treatment of t-SNE 'false positives'.

The key technical observation (t-SNE's exact invariance under additive shifts of squared interpoint distances, Lemma 16) is clean, correct as far as I can verify, and yields several surprising corollaries: arbitrarily unclustered impostor datasets producing identical stationary outputs (Theorem 3, Corollary 4), near-identical inputs producing arbitrarily different outputs (Theorem 5), and Lemma 6, which is genuinely striking.

Theorem 8 is the more substantive technical contribution: an input-agnostic, quantitative upper bound (α ≈ 3) on how extreme an outlier any stationary t-SNE embedding can depict, derived via a careful gradient/affinity-asymmetry analysis (Lemmas 19–20).

The paper connects theory to practice with concrete constructions (Algorithm 1 for impostor datasets, poison-point attacks) and demonstrations on real datasets (PBMC3k, credit card fraud, BBC News embeddings), and appropriately contrasts t-SNE's behavior with PCA.
The related work section is thorough and honestly situates the contribution relative to prior empirical criticisms (Yang et al., Chari & Pachter, Snoeck et al.).
weaknesses: The core technical engine is elementary. Lemma 16 is a two-line algebraic cancellation in the Gaussian kernel, and Theorems 3, 5, 9, 11 follow from it via routine intermediate-value/continuity arguments. For a paper whose headline claim is 'provably', the proof depth is thin; the main novelty is noticing a simple invariance, not a difficult analysis.

Significant gap between theory and the claimed practical implications. All main theorems concern the set of stationary points of the idealized, exact t-SNE objective, whereas practitioners run gradient descent with early exaggeration, momentum, and (for large n) Barnes-Hut approximations. Showing that a perfectly clustered Y is *a* stationary point of an unclustered input does not establish that the algorithm will converge to it; the leap from 'exists in the stationary set' to 't-SNE outputs this' is bridged only by a handful of anecdotal figures.

The 'WLOG D = n−1' assumption (footnote 1) is not actually without loss of generality. Real datasets have fixed, often much smaller ambient dimension D, and the additive-shift construction (Lemma 15, Schoenberg embedding) produces impostors in R^{n−1}; whether comparable impostors exist in the original ambient space is not addressed, weakening the practical relevance of Theorem 3 for real data.

A conceptual concern about the framing: silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, and Dunn indices are not scale-invariant, and the impostor construction is precisely an affine rescaling of the input distances. One can argue the 'unclustered impostor' is in a meaningful sense the same data under a different metric scaling, so the conclusion 'cluster strength cannot be inferred' partly reflects the choice of scale-sensitive indices rather than a fundamental failure of the visualization.

The novelty claim ('first work which theoretically analyzes some of the key limitations of t-SNE') is overstated: Snoeck et al. (2025) already give theoretical impossibility results for constant-dimension embeddings, and the folk understanding that t-SNE fabricates cluster structure has been empirically documented for years (e.g., Wattenberg et al.'s widely known guidance on spurious clusters, which is not cited).

The evaluation, while illustrative, is not systematic: no UMAP or other modern baseline comparisons, no quantitative protocol for the adversarial experiments beyond silhouette scores, no ablations over perplexity or dimensionality for the real-data claims, and the empirical section reads as a collection of curated examples.

Presentation issues: the GitHub code link is blank ('available on Github at .'), harming reproducibility; and the proof of Theorem 8 contains dense, hard-to-verify chains of inequalities where several intermediate steps (e.g., the use of Lemma 19 bounds and the 1/(2n) normalization argument) deserve more careful exposition.

The discussion of when additive invariance is *not* harmful (robustness to concentrated noise, Figure 6) is relegated to a paragraph and left as future work, giving an incomplete picture of when the identified failure modes actually bite versus when t-SNE is well-behaved.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: the paper provides, to the authors' knowledge and credibly so, the first systematic theoretical analysis of t-SNE's 'false positive' behavior (fabricated clusters, suppressed outliers), complementing the existing positive guarantees (Arora et al. 2018; Linderman & Steinerberger 2019).

The key technical insight — that t-SNE is invariant under additive shifting of squared interpoint distances (Lemma 16, proved cleanly via the ratio structure of Gaussian affinities and Schoenberg's embedding theorem) — is simple, surprising, and leads to strong impossibility results (Theorems 3, 5, Lemma 6): an arbitrarily unclustered 'impostor' dataset can share all stationary points with a highly clustered one.

Theorem 8 gives a quantitative, input-agnostic bound (α(Y) ≤ 3 + o(1)) showing t-SNE provably cannot depict extreme outliers, with a proof based on the asymmetry between input and output affinities; this is a genuinely useful, checkable result.

Good theory-practice bridge: the theoretical constructions are made practical (Algorithm 1 for impostor datasets) and demonstrated on real datasets (PBMC3k single-cell data, credit card fraud, BBC News embeddings), with PCA as a meaningful control showing these failure modes are specific to t-SNE rather than generic to 2D embedding.

The connection between additive invariance and concentration of measure in high dimensions (Figures 2, 6) explains why these failure modes are not pathological edge cases but plausibly affect real high-dimensional data, and yields a striking single-poison-point adversarial attack.

Well-written and well-organized: the implications of each theorem are carefully explained for practitioners, related work is thorough and honest about prior empirical criticisms (Chari & Pachter 2023, Yang et al. 2021, Snoeck et al. 2025).
weaknesses: The central observation (additive invariance of P under shifts of squared distances) is nearly immediate from the definition of the Gaussian affinities; the perceived novelty rests on the consequences rather than technical depth. Some may view parts of the message (t-SNE does not preserve global structure/distances) as close to known folk wisdom, e.g., Wattenberg et al.'s practical guidance and Chari & Pachter (2023), with the contribution being formalization.

All theoretical results concern the set of stationary points of the idealized objective; practical t-SNE uses early exaggeration and finite gradient descent, so the provable statements apply only partially to what practitioners actually compute. The empirical results partially mitigate this, but the gap between 'all stationary points coincide' and 'the algorithm's output coincides' is not formally addressed.

Some experimental claims are visually anecdotal: e.g., 'PCA largely succeeds' on the fraud subset is asserted from plots of a 5050-point random subset without quantitative metrics (e.g., outlier-detection AUC) or multiple seeds/runs; Table 1's comparison of silhouette in a 2D embedding vs. 100D input is partly expected for any embedding method and would benefit from more systematic baselines (UMAP, Isomap, etc.).

Minor technical/editorial issues: Theorem 11 contains a typo (ϵ bounded by DI(X_ϵ) instead of DI(X)); the '= 3 + o(1)' phrasing in Theorem 8 is loose; the GitHub link is missing in the text; Corollary 4's restriction to even n and the singleton-cluster caveats deserve a remark on generality.

The paper does not explore mitigations or constructive guidance (e.g., diagnostics that would distinguish real from impostor clusterings, or parameter regimes where failure modes are mitigated), which limits actionable impact beyond 'do not trust t-SNE for cluster strength or outliers.'

strengths: First systematic *theoretical* analysis of t-SNE's failure modes (false positives, false negatives, outlier misrepresentation), complementing the existing positive guarantees (Arora et al. 2018; Linderman & Steinerberger 2019); this fills a genuine gap in the literature.

Clean and elegant technical core: the additive/multiplicative invariance of t-SNE under shifts of squared interpoint distances (Lemmas 16-18) yields a family of strong results (Theorems 3, 5, Lemma 6, Corollary 4) with short, verifiable proofs; the outlier bound (Theorem 9, α(Y) ≤ 3.266 + o(1)) is a novel and input-agnostic impossibility result with a self-contained proof via a careful gradient asymmetry argument.

The negative results are complemented by constructive, practically realizable procedures (Algorithm 1 for impostor datasets; the poison-point construction), and demonstrated convincingly on real datasets (PBMC3k single-cell data, BBC News with RoBERTa embeddings, credit card fraud), with PCA and UMAP as informative baselines/contrasts.

The paper explains *why* the failures occur (additive invariance; input/output affinity asymmetry), connecting the theory to the concentration-of-measure regime of real high-dimensional data, which strengthens the practical relevance of the worst-case constructions.

Well written and well positioned: the related work carefully distinguishes known empirical criticisms (Yang et al. 2021; Chari & Pachter 2023; Schubert & Gertz 2017) from the new formal contributions, and honestly attributes the additive invariance observation to Lee & Verleysen (2011).
weaknesses: The central mechanism (additive invariance of SNE-type methods) was already identified by Lee & Verleysen (2011; 2014); the novelty of the cluster-salience section lies mainly in formalizing its consequences (Theorems 3, 5, Lemma 6) rather than the underlying observation itself.

The theoretical results concern the set of *all stationary points* of the t-SNE objective, whereas practical t-SNE returns a specific local minimum found via early exaggeration + gradient descent; the link between the impossibility results for stationary points and the behavior of the deployed algorithm is established only empirically, not theoretically.

Several results are worst-case/existential: Theorem 7 (poison point) holds only for ρ = 1, and Theorem 9's constant 3.266 depends on an admittedly ad hoc thresholded outlier definition (max{1, diam}); the practical significance relies on the accompanying experiments rather than the theorem statements themselves.

A few minor presentation issues: some theorem statements contain typos (e.g., '1 < ϵ ≤ DI(X_ϵ; ...)' in Theorem 12 should presumably reference DI(X; ...)), the UMAP/poison-point experiments in the appendix are described as 'preliminary,' and the outlier-number definition with multiple outliers is only sketched.

No quantitative methodology is given for how representative the adversarial constructions are of 'typical' datasets beyond the Gaussian/concentration arguments; a skeptic could argue the impostor/poison-point regimes are contrived, though the real-data experiments partially answer this.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and under-explored question: what information can NOT be reliably inferred from a t-SNE plot? This complements existing positive guarantees (Arora et al. 2018; Linderman & Steinerberger 2019) and is relevant to practitioners in single-cell genomics, NLP interpretability, etc.

The core technical insight is clean and well-executed: t-SNE's input affinities are invariant under additive shifts of squared interpoint distances (Lemma 17), which elegantly yields Theorem 3, Corollary 4, Theorem 5, and Lemma 6 (near-simplex inputs generate ALL stationary outputs). The proofs in Appendix A.6 are self-contained and appear correct, including the Schoenberg-embeddability argument.

Theorem 9 (outlier suppression, α(Y) ≤ 3.266 + o_n(1)) is a nontrivial quantitative result with a complete proof chain (Lemmas 21, 22), and the intuition about input/output affinity asymmetry is well motivated.

The paper connects theory to practice convincingly in places: the PBMC3k 'impostor dataset' experiment (Figure 2), the single poison-point attack (Figures 4, 10), the credit card fraud and BBC news case studies (Figures 5, 6, 15), and robustness checks under PCA pre-processing (Figures 7-8) and increasing dataset size.

Good breadth of comparison: PCA and UMAP are used as references throughout (Appendices A.3, B.2), the results are stated for multiple cluster-quality indices (silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn), and code is stated to be available on GitHub.
The writing is generally clear, and the discussion (Section 6) is appropriately balanced, acknowledging that additive invariance may also filter high-dimensional noise (Lee & Verleysen; El Karoui).
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central mechanism. The key enabling property — invariance of t-SNE affinities under additive shifts of squared distances — is explicitly credited to Lee & Verleysen (2011, Section 4). The main theorems (3, 5, 6, and the cluster-salience corollaries) are essentially immediate consequences of this known invariance combined with continuity/IVT arguments. The contribution is more a formalization of known properties than a new technical idea, which weakens the claim of being 'the first work which theoretically analyzes the key limitations of t-SNE.'

Significant theory-practice gap. All theorems concern exact stationary points of the population t-SNE objective, whereas practitioners use gradient descent with early exaggeration, momentum, learning-rate schedules, and Barnes-Hut approximations, none of which the theory covers. The paper does not establish that the constructed impostor datasets or poison points reliably affect typical algorithmic outputs beyond illustrative examples; the empirical sections are largely anecdotal (hand-crafted adversarial cases) rather than systematic (no distributions over random datasets, no success-rate statistics for the attack, no hyperparameter sweeps).

The constant in Theorem 9 (α ≤ 3.266) is loose relative to the empirically observed suppression (α ≲ 0.2 in practice), and the outlier definition (Definition 8) with its ad hoc max{1, diam} thresholding and hyperplane-margin formulation feels engineered to make the proof go through rather than to capture a natural notion of outlyingness.

Constructive results assume inputs embeddable in R^{n-1} with arbitrary squared-distance matrices; real datasets do not have this freedom. The bridge to real data (MDS-based impostor construction, Algorithm 1) is provided but the resulting failure is demonstrated only on a handful of datasets, and the paper does not characterize when high-dimensional real data actually falls in the near-simplex regime beyond citing concentration-of-measure folklore.

Limited practical guidance. The paper concludes that one should take t-SNE plots 'with a grain of salt' and that t-SNE is 'the wrong tool' for outlier detection, but offers no constructive remedy, no diagnostic to detect when a given plot may be misleading, and no quantitative decision procedure — a notable omission given the paper's emphasis on downstream scientific consequences.

Some presentation issues: the main text repeatedly asserts practical relevance of stationary-point statements ('this is experimentally corroborated') where the experiments only show qualitative similarity at particular parameter settings; several figures are small and hard to read; and the contribution list (e.g., 'adversarial attack') oversells results that are existence constructions for stationary points rather than demonstrated attacks on deployed pipelines.

strengths: First formal, systematic theoretical treatment of t-SNE's failure modes (false positives, false negatives, outlier suppression), complementing the existing positive guarantees of Arora et al. (2018) and Linderman & Steinerberger (2019).

The core mathematical insight — additive invariance of t-SNE under shifts of squared interpoint distances — is used to derive clean impossibility results (Theorems 3, 5, 7) showing that cluster salience cannot be inferred from the output and that identical outputs arise from arbitrarily weakly separated 'impostor' datasets.

Theorem 9 is a genuinely novel, input-agnostic bound (α(Y) ≤ 3.266 + o_n(1)) proving that no stationary t-SNE embedding can depict extreme outliers; the gradient-based proof (Lemmas 21-22) is self-contained and technically sound.

Strong empirical grounding: experiments on real datasets (PBMC3k single-cell, credit card fraud, BBC News with RoBERTa embeddings) plus synthetic data, with useful comparisons against PCA and UMAP that contextualize when t-SNE fails (e.g., PCA preserves α-outlier numbers while t-SNE does not).

The 'poison point' adversarial attack (Theorem 7) is a memorable and practically relevant result, with a clean proof via exact P-matrix equivalence at ρ=1 and experimental corroboration at realistic perplexities.

Well written and clearly organized; the discussion candidly identifies the two underlying mechanisms (additive invariance, input/output affinity asymmetry) and acknowledges prior observations (Lee & Verleysen 2011, Schubert & Gertz 2017, Yang et al. 2021). Results are shown to generalize across multiple cluster indices (silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Dunn).
weaknesses: The key mechanism (additive shift invariance of squared distances) is already known from Lee & Verleysen (2011), and the paper admits this; Theorems 3 and 5 are essentially corollaries of this known property (Theorem 5's proof is 'immediate'), so the novelty is concentrated in packaging and in Theorem 9 rather than in the core lemma.

All theoretical results are stated for exact stationary points of the unexaggerated t-SNE objective, whereas practical t-SNE uses early exaggeration and gradient descent that does not converge to stationary points of L; the gap between the idealized definition of t-SNEρ(X) and actual algorithmic output is bridged only empirically.

The results are worst-case existence/adversarial constructions; the paper does not quantify how frequently natural (non-adversarial) datasets exhibit these failure modes, which limits the strength of the practical warnings.
Theorem 7 is proven only for the degenerate case ρ=1; degradation for typical perplexity values is shown only experimentally, not theoretically.

The choice of outlier/cluster-strength metrics (silhouette score, the thresholded α-outlier definition) is somewhat arbitrary, and the constant 3.266 in Theorem 9 is loose; conclusions could be metric-dependent.
The GitHub URL for the code appears blank in the manuscript, which weakens reproducibility claims as submitted.
